claims.text: Plastic deformation under uniaxial tension in quaternary equiatomic FCC alloys is governed by dislocation glide on {111} planes.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate when thermal activation of dislocation motion is negligible relative to the applied driving stress.
The strain-rate-insensitive regime typically occurs at very low temperatures or extremely high strain rates.
The initial material is a solutionized, single-phase quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy.
The relevant mobile dislocations have Burgers vectors of type a/2<110>.
Plastic flow is controlled by dislocation glide subject to lattice friction and solute drag.
A small activation volume leads to athermal yielding at particular strain-rate and temperature combinations.
Yield strength has a logarithmic dependence on strain rate at moderate temperatures.
Yield strength plateaus at low temperatures or high strain rates because thermal assistance is insufficient to overcome lattice resistance.
Standard dislocation theory for FCC metals treats yield strength as thermally activated.
The proposed deformation hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC structures.
Deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation or twinning would introduce strain-rate dependencies different from those of the proposed dislocation-glide regime.
New diffraction peaks or peak splitting during tension can indicate a deformation-induced phase transformation.
Diffraction peak broadening during tension can indicate an increase in dislocation density.
Observation of increasing secondary-phase fraction concurrent with yielding would falsify a purely dislocation-glide-based explanation.
